newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Germany, France discuss Bosnia peacekeeping.
newsitem.headline: Germany, France discuss Bosnia peacekeeping.

text.p: Germany is keen to send peacekeeping troops to Bosnia and is discussing with France how best this may be done, German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said in Sarajevo on Wednesday.
If the NATO allies decide to deploy a follow-up force in the former Yugoslav republic after their peacekeeping mandate expires on December 20, Germany wants to play a meaningful role, Ruehe said.
Such a follow-up force, which has not yet been agreed by NATO political leaders, should however have its own mandate restricted to no more than a year, he said.
Germany currently contributes 3,400 troops, mainly support units, to the 58,000-strong NATO peace implementation force (IFOR), and these are based in Croatia rather than Bosnia.
Germany wants its armed forces to play a more mainstream role in international peacekeeping operations after decades of avoiding military involvement abrod.
But the deployment of German troops to the Balkans remains a sensitive issue. Memories of its World War Two occupation of Yugoslavia have not faded.
"If there is a follow-up force, Germany will be part of it," Ruehe told a Sarajevo news conference. "We have started talks within the framework of the Franco-German brigade."
The brigade was set up by Paris and Bonn as the embryo of a future European defence force, the Eurocorps. It has now expanded to include units from other European nations.
He said a consensus in favour of German involvement in peacekeeping operations in Bosnia had developed at home and other NATO nations were also keen.

With a successor peacekeeping force estimated at about 25,000-strong, Ruehe indicated he saw a German contribution of between 2,000 and 3,000, with the configuration of the German force worked out in talks with the French.
Ruehe was speaking during a joint tour with British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo of British and German peacekeeping troops in Bosnia and Croatia.
Portillo stressed there was still no commitment to a follow-on force. But he said the political groundwork could be laid at a meeting of NATO defence ministers in Norway later this month.
"We can take the first steps towards taking a NATO-wide decision on a follow-up force," Portillo said.

While NATO leaders are anxious to avoid putting any embarrassing pressure on the United States to commit itself to a successor force in the run-up to the presidential election, Portillo made clear he expected Washington to join in.
"If there were to be a follow-up force, America would have to be part of it," he said. "NATO came in together, NATO is serving together and NATO will leave together."
The two ministers' visit coincided with Bosnia's first post-war elections, and both pronounced themselves broadly satisfied with the way the poll had been run.
